883.title: Tanakh
883.hook: Torah, Prophets and Writings, twenty-four books in the Jewish count
883.howItsDone: In synagogue the Torah is read from a handwritten scroll, portion by portion, in order, a passage from the Prophets called the haftarah is read with it, and some of the Writings, such as Esther on Purim, are read on particular days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, we reached the last word of the Hebrew Bible: ve-ya'al, and let him go up. Your line was the call to keep climbing. What small step up did you take? Today, we step back and look at the whole shelf. Day eight hundred eighty-three.

One word on the spine of a Jewish Bible: Tanakh. It isn't a name of a person or a place. It's a sort of table of contents squeezed into one word. All along this path we've been walking through it: the creation and the patriarchs, Moses and the wilderness, judges and kings, prophets, poems, Job's arguments, Esther's banquet, Daniel in Babylon, Ezra and Nehemiah rebuilding. Yesterday we turned the last page. So today, before anything else, it's worth knowing what the whole thing is called, and how it's put together.
screen: `ONE WORD ON THE SPINE.` → `A TABLE OF CONTENTS IN A WORD.` → `THE LAST PAGE IS TURNED.`

segments.voice: Tanakh is built from the first letters of its three parts: T, N, K. T is for Torah, teaching: the books of Moses, from Genesis to Deuteronomy. This is the scroll that sits in the ark in a synagogue and is read aloud, portion by portion. N is for Nevi'im, Prophets. That includes the stories of Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings, and then the books of the prophets themselves: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the shorter prophets, which tradition counts together as one book called the Twelve. K is for Ketuvim, Writings: Psalms, Proverbs and Job, the scrolls like Ruth, Esther and Ecclesiastes, then Daniel, Ezra and Nehemiah, and Chronicles at the close. Take Samuel as one book, Kings as one, the Twelve as one, Ezra and Nehemiah as one, and Chronicles as one, and you reach the number Jewish tradition gives: twenty-four books. The Talmud also records an order for the Prophets and the Writings. So when you hear Tanakh, hear a library with three rooms. The first room is the teaching itself. The second is the story of what happened when a people tried to live it, and the prophets who called them back. The third is everything else a people needs: songs, wisdom, love poetry, grief, history, and hard questions. Notice that the rooms aren't the same in the life of the synagogue. The Torah is read from the scroll in order, week by week. Passages from the Prophets are read alongside it. Some of the Writings come out on particular days, like Esther on Purim. One library, three rooms, used in different ways.
screen: `T, N, K: THREE INITIALS.` · then, large: `TORAH, NEVI'IM, KETUVIM.` · `COUNTED AS TWENTY-FOUR BOOKS.` · then: `THREE ROOMS, USED DIFFERENTLY.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to name the three parts. Sit, and breathe in slowly. On the out-breath, say silently: Torah, teaching. Breathe in again. On the out-breath: Nevi'im, Prophets. Once more. On the out-breath: Ketuvim, Writings. Now go around again, and with each name let one story from that room come to mind, any one you remember from this path. A story from the Torah. A story from the Prophets. A story from the Writings. If you pray, you can give thanks in words from your tradition for something you learned from them. The bell holds the time.
Tanakh. The Hebrew Bible's own name, built from its three parts: Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim, teaching, Prophets and Writings. Today's word.
Your line: three parts, one library. Today, tell someone what the three letters of Tanakh stand for. Day eight hundred eighty-three.

what a scholar hears: books that are split in other counts, like Samuel, Kings and the Twelve, count as one each, giving the traditional twenty-four.

884.title: Argued into the canon
884.hook: the Mishnah records debates over whether Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes belonged (Yadayim 3:5)
884.carry: a doubt didn't throw a book out
884.howItsDone: Jewish study keeps disagreements on the page: the Mishnah and the Talmud record minority opinions by name alongside the rulings, and students learn the arguments as well as the outcomes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Tanakh: Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim. Your line was three parts, one library. Could you name all three? Today, a question about that library: who decided what went on the shelves, and did everyone agree? Day eight hundred eighty-four.

The minutes of the meeting were kept. That's the surprising thing. A library of holy books could have been handed down as if it had always been settled, with no trace of a quarrel. Instead, the rabbis of the Mishnah and the Talmud wrote down the arguments. Which books are holy? Does this one belong? What do we do with a book that seems to contradict itself? And they didn't only keep the winning side. They kept the names of the people who doubted. Earlier on this path, we heard Rabbi Akiva call the Song of Songs the holy of holies. Today, the other half of that page: the argument he was answering.
screen: `THE MINUTES WERE KEPT.` → `WHICH BOOKS ARE HOLY?` → `THE DOUBTERS ARE NAMED.`

segments.voice: The Mishnah, in tractate Yadayim, uses a strange phrase for scripture: a holy book is one that makes the hands unclean. Then it records a disagreement, almost like a transcript. One rabbi says: the Song of Songs makes the hands unclean, but about Ecclesiastes there's a dispute. Another says the reverse: Ecclesiastes doesn't, and about the Song of Songs there's a dispute. A third connects the question to the old schools of Shammai and Hillel. Another reports a ruling that both books do make the hands unclean. Only then comes Akiva's strong answer: no one in Israel, he insists, ever disputed the Song of Songs; if there was a dispute, it was over Ecclesiastes. The Talmud adds more. In tractate Shabbat it says the sages wanted to store Ecclesiastes away, to hide it, because its words seemed to contradict each other. One verse praises something, another seems to dismiss it. Why didn't they? Because, the Talmud says, its beginning is words of Torah and its end is words of Torah. And the book does end that way, in the King James words: "Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man." So the hard middle was kept because of its frame. Put it together and something stands out. These books weren't slipped into the canon quietly. They were argued into it, out loud, and the record of the argument became part of the tradition too. In this record, a doubt didn't throw a book out; it made the sages look at its first and last lines. Ecclesiastes stayed on the shelf with its hard middle intact, and the doubt stayed on the page beside it.
screen: `BOOKS THAT MAKE THE HANDS UNCLEAN.` · `A DISPUTE OVER TWO BOOKS.` · then, large: `ITS BEGINNING AND END ARE TORAH.` · then: `ARGUED IN, OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to appreciate one debated book. Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Choose one of the two: the Song of Songs, with its love poetry, or Ecclesiastes, with its hard questions. Bring to mind one line you remember from it. If nothing comes, here's one from Ecclesiastes in the King James words: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." Hold the line. Now ask: what would make someone doubt this book belongs? Then ask: what would make someone fight to keep it? Let both answers sit side by side. If you pray, you can give thanks in words from your tradition for the books that were kept. The bell holds the time.
Kohelet. The Hebrew name of Ecclesiastes, one of the books the rabbis argued over before keeping it on the shelf. Today's word.
Your line: a doubt didn't throw a book out. Today, when you doubt something you value, look at it more closely before you set it aside. Day eight hundred eighty-four.

what it means: the rabbis argued over whether the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes belonged, and kept the record of the argument.

885.title: Four levels of reading
885.hook: the plain meaning, the hint, the teaching and the secret: pardes
885.howItsDone: Jewish Bibles are studied with commentaries printed around the text, such as Rashi, which give the plain meaning and rabbinic teachings side by side, and students learn to say which kind of reading they are offering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes were argued into the canon, and the argument was kept. Your line was a doubt didn't throw a book out. What did you look at more closely? Today, now that the books are on the shelf: how do you read them? Day eight hundred eighty-five.

An orchard. In the Song of Songs, the lover says, in the King James words, "Thy plants are an orchard of pomegranates, with pleasant fruits." The Hebrew word there for orchard is pardes. Much later, Jewish readers took that same word and turned it into a map for reading scripture. Its four consonants, P, R, D, S, became the first letters of four ways into a text. So a single verse becomes an orchard: you can walk in at the gate and see the trees, or go deeper and find what's growing underneath. Today we take the walk, and we learn which gate comes first.
screen: `AN ORCHARD OF POMEGRANATES.` → `PARDES: P, R, D, S.` → `FOUR WAYS INTO A TEXT.`

segments.voice: Here are the four. P is peshat: the plain meaning, what the words say in their own setting. R is remez: the hint, a meaning pointed to by a detail, a number, a strange word choice. D is derash: the teaching drawn out by searching the text, the way the rabbis of the midrash read it, finding lessons and stories in its gaps. And S is sod: the secret, the hidden meaning the mystics looked for. Take the Song of Songs. Its peshat is a love poem between two people. Its derash, in rabbinic tradition, is the love between God and the people of Israel. Both readings live side by side. But there's an order. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, records a short rule: a verse does not depart from its plain meaning. You can read deeper, but you can't read past the words as if they weren't there. Plain meaning first. The commentator Rashi, in his note on Genesis 3:8, says he has come only for the plain sense of the verse, and for the midrash that helps settle its words. The same rule works far from any scroll. A text, a message, a friend's sentence can all be read for hidden meanings before anyone has read what they actually say. The orchard has deep roots, but you enter through the gate. Before you hunt for the hint, the teaching or the secret, ask the plain question first: what do these words say?
screen: `PESHAT, REMEZ, DERASH, SOD.` · `ONE SONG, TWO READINGS.` · then, large: `A VERSE KEEPS ITS PLAIN MEANING.` · then: `ENTER THROUGH THE GATE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to read one verse two ways. Sit, and settle your breath. Take a line from a few days ago, the last words of the Hebrew Bible: ve-ya'al, and let him go up. First, the plain meaning. Cyrus, king of Persia, tells the exiles they may go up to Jerusalem and rebuild. Say it to yourself simply, and stay there a while. Then, only after that, let a second reading come, a teaching drawn from it: what would going up mean in your own life today? Keep the two readings side by side, without letting the second erase the first. If you pray, you can ask in words from your tradition for clear eyes when you read. The bell holds the time.
Peshat. The plain meaning of a verse, the first of the four ways into the orchard: peshat, remez, derash, sod. Today's word.
Your line: plain meaning first. Today, before you read between the lines of a message, read the lines themselves. Day eight hundred eighty-five.

screen: `DAY 885 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EVERY WORD HAS A TUNE.`

886.title: Every word has a tune
886.hook: the Tanakh is chanted with ancient musical notes
886.carry: where the verse breathes is where its thought divides
886.howItsDone: In synagogue, a reader chants the Torah and haftarah portions from the text using the te'amim, and young people preparing for a bar or bat mitzvah learn the trope to chant their portion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the orchard of four readings: peshat, remez, derash, sod. Your line was plain meaning first. Did you read a message for what it actually said? Today, the last day of our time in the Writings, and a way of reading you hear with your ears. Day eight hundred eighty-six.

Tiny marks, above and below the letters. Open a printed Hebrew Bible and look closely: besides the letters, and the vowel dots, there's a third layer of small signs scattered across the verses. A little wedge here, a curl there, a dot beside a line. Those marks are the trope, in Hebrew te'amim. They tell a reader how to chant. The Torah scroll itself has no vowels and no marks at all, so the reader learns them beforehand. In the synagogue, the Torah is chanted, word by word, each word carrying its own short phrase of melody, and the marks say which phrase. So this whole library we've been reading, the Torah, the Prophets, the Writings, carries its music on the page.
screen: `A THIRD LAYER OF MARKS.` → `TROPE: TE'AMIM.` → `THE TEXT IS SUNG.`

segments.voice: The trope does two jobs at once. The first is music: each mark is a little melody, and a verse becomes a chain of them. The second is sense. The same marks work like punctuation. Some say pause here, strongly. Some say keep going, these words belong together. So the tune is also a guide to meaning: where the verse breathes is where its thought divides. Take the first verse of the Torah, in the King James words: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." In the Hebrew, the main pause mark falls after God created, and the chant rests there, before the heaven and the earth. Read it with the tune, and the verse has a shape. The Hebrew word ta'am, the singular of te'amim, can mean taste, and also sense or reason. And here's a link back to the water gate. When the book of Nehemiah says the Levites read distinctly, gave the sense, and caused the people to understand the reading, the Talmud reads part of that verse as the te'amim themselves. On that reading, understanding the text and hearing where it divides go together. One more thing. Tradition has more than one melody for the same marks, and some books, like Esther on Purim and Lamentations on the ninth of Av, have tunes of their own. Same marks, many voices. Lately we've walked through the Writings: wisdom, song, lament, Esther, Daniel, Ezra and Nehemiah, Chronicles. Today, the marks that carry all of it as song.
screen: `MARKS THAT ARE MUSIC.` · `MARKS THAT ARE PUNCTUATION.` · then, large: `WHERE IT BREATHES, IT DIVIDES.` · then: `SAME MARKS, MANY MELODIES.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to listen to one chanted verse. Sit, and let the room go quiet. If you've ever heard Torah chanted, at a synagogue, a bar or bat mitzvah, a recording, let a few notes of it come back now. If you haven't, take the first verse of Genesis and say it slowly to yourself, pausing after God created, then going on: the heaven and the earth. Listen to where the pause falls. Say it again, and let your voice rise and fall a little, any way that feels natural. After the bell, if you'd like, find one recording of a chanted verse and listen with your eyes closed. The bell holds the time.
Trope. The small marks in the Hebrew text that give each word its melody and show where the verse pauses: in Hebrew, te'amim. Today's word.
Your line: where the verse breathes is where its thought divides. Today, read one sentence that matters to you out loud, slowly, and listen for where it wants to pause. Day eight hundred eighty-six.

887.title: After the last page
887.hook: the Tanakh closes, and Jewish history goes on
887.carry: the pages ran out; the handing-on didn't
887.howItsDone: Jews read and study the Tanakh alongside the teachings of the rabbis who came after it, and some communities study Pirkei Avot, which opens with the chain of tradition from Moses, on Sabbath afternoons in the weeks after Passover.

segments.voice: Yesterday, trope: the small marks above and below the letters that tell a reader how to chant. Your line was where the verse breathes is where its thought divides. Did one verse reach you as a song? Today, the music stops at the end of the book, and something else starts. Day eight hundred eighty-seven.

Close a Tanakh and look at the last printed page. A few days ago we heard its final words: Cyrus's call to the exiles, let him go up. Then white space. Maybe a blank leaf before the cover. And yet the people in that book did not stop on that page. Somebody went up. Somebody rebuilt a wall, planted a vineyard, argued with a neighbor, married, buried a parent, taught a child to read the very scroll that had just run out of pages. A book can end. A people keeps waking up the next morning. Today we step off the last page into the long stretch of Jewish life the Bible itself never narrates.
screen: `THE LAST PRINTED PAGE.` → `THEN WHITE SPACE.` → `A PEOPLE WAKES UP THE NEXT DAY.`

segments.voice: Start with how the library is shelved. The Talmud, in tractate Bava Batra, lays out an order: the Prophets close with the Twelve, the short books like Malachi, and the Writings close with Chronicles. So the Tanakh has more than one ending, and each one leans forward. Malachi's last lines tell the people to remember the teaching of Moses, and then make a promise. In the King James words: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD." The Prophets end with someone still on the way. At Passover, some families pour a cup for Elijah and open the door. A book that ends with a guest who hasn't arrived. Then a harder turn. The Talmud, in tractate Yoma, says that when the last prophets, Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi, died, the holy spirit of prophecy departed from Israel. No more prophets. But the same passage adds that people still heard a bat kol, an echo of a heavenly voice. Quieter, but not silence. So who carries the story now? The opening of Pirkei Avot answers with a chain. Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and the prophets to the men of the Great Assembly. And those men gave three pieces of advice: be careful in judgment, raise up many students, and build a fence around the Torah. Notice the second one. When the prophets go quiet, the answer is students. The pages ran out. The handing-on didn't.
screen: `MORE THAN ONE ENDING.` · then, large: `I WILL SEND YOU ELIJAH THE PROPHET.` · `PROPHECY GOES QUIET.` · `A CHAIN OF HANDS: RAISE UP STUDENTS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: think of what came after a story ended. Settle, and let your breath slow down. Bring to mind one ending in your own life. A graduation, a move, a funeral, the last day at a job, a friendship that closed. At the time, it may have seemed like the last page. Now look at the morning after. What did you do that first ordinary day? Who handed you something, or who did you hand something to? Stay with that next morning for a while. If you pray, you can use words from your own tradition to give thanks for what continued. The bell holds the time.
Bat kol. An echo of a heavenly voice, still heard, the Talmud says, after the Tanakh closed and prophecy went quiet. Today's word.
Your line: the pages ran out; the handing-on didn't. Today, hand one thing on: a recipe, a skill, a story from your family, to someone who will carry it after you. Day eight hundred eighty-seven.

888.title: Greeks arrive
888.hook: Alexander reaches the land, and Greek culture spreads
888.howItsDone: Jewish students learn the saying of Shimon the Righteous in Pirkei Avot, that the world stands on Torah, service and acts of loving-kindness, and the Talmud's legend of his meeting with Alexander is told in study of the Second Temple period.

segments.voice: Yesterday we stepped off the last page of the Tanakh, and the chain of teachers picked it up. Your line was the pages ran out; the handing-on didn't. What did you hand on? Today a king from Macedonia walks into that story. Day eight hundred eighty-eight.

The first book of Maccabees opens at a gallop. Alexander, son of Philip, the Macedonian, comes out of the land the book calls Chettiim, defeats Darius, king of the Persians, and keeps going. He takes cities, kills kings, and goes to the ends of the earth, until, in the King James words, "the earth was quiet before him." Then, a few verses later, he falls sick, knows he is dying, and divides his kingdom among his servants. The book says he reigned twelve years. That's the whole of Alexander in that chapter: a storm that passes. But what he left behind did not pass. Greek language, Greek cities, Greek ways of living arrive in the land of Israel and stay.
screen: `A KING FROM MACEDONIA.` → `THE EARTH WAS QUIET BEFORE HIM.` → `THE STORM PASSES. THE CULTURE STAYS.`

segments.voice: The Talmud, in tractate Yoma, tells the meeting as a legend. Alexander's army is marching toward Jerusalem. The high priest, Shimon the Righteous, puts on his priestly garments, and with the leaders of the city carrying torches, walks all night to meet him. When Alexander sees him, the conqueror gets down from his chariot and bows. His men are shocked. Alexander explains: this is the face I see before me when I win my battles. The Temple is spared. It's a story about two worlds meeting, and the surprise is who bows. Now remember yesterday's chain. Shimon the Righteous is the man Pirkei Avot names right after the Great Assembly, the one who said the world stands on three things: Torah, service, and acts of loving-kindness. So the legend puts the heir of the chain face to face with the man who conquered the world. But meeting isn't always bowing. Back in the first book of Maccabees, some in Israel say, let's make a covenant with the nations around us, and they build a place of exercise in Jerusalem after the customs of the nations. The book is not pleased. Two cultures meet, and the meeting goes in every direction at once: respect, borrowing, worry, conflict. The Hebrew name for Greece, Yavan, turns up in the book of Daniel too: the kingdom of Yavan is the one that comes after Persia. For the next few days, the question underneath these stories is the same: how do you live inside someone else's culture and stay yourself?
screen: `THE CONQUEROR BOWS.` · then, large: `TORAH, SERVICE, LOVING-KINDNESS.` · `A PLACE OF EXERCISE IN JERUSALEM.` · `INSIDE A CULTURE, STILL YOURSELF?`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to notice one Greek idea in your life. Settle and breathe. Let your mind walk through an ordinary day: the gym, a class, a word you use, a game you watch, a way you argue or vote. Find one thing you suspect came to you from Greek culture, and if you're not sure, that's fine, just hold the question. Then ask the second question: what in your life came from your own family, your own people, your own tradition? Let both sit side by side for a while, without picking a winner. If you pray, you can use words from your tradition for the places you live. The bell holds the time.
Greeks arrive. Alexander sweeps through, and Greek language and ways of life settle into the land of Israel. Today's word.
Your line: two cultures meet. Today, when you meet someone from a world unlike yours, notice one thing to respect and one thing you'd keep as your own. Day eight hundred eighty-eight.

889.title: The Torah in Greek
889.hook: the Torah is translated into Greek; legend says by seventy-two elders
889.carry: something always stays behind in the original
889.howItsDone: Jews today read the Torah in Hebrew in the synagogue and study it in many languages, often with a translation printed beside the Hebrew; the Talmud's story of the seventy-two elders is taught in tractate Megillah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Alexander came through like a storm, and in the legend he bowed to the high priest. Your line was two cultures meet. Where did you notice the meeting? Today, the Torah itself crosses into Greek. Day eight hundred eighty-nine.

A king sends for seventy-two elders. That's how the Talmud tells it, in tractate Megillah. King Ptolemy gathers them, and before they can talk to each other, he puts each one in a separate house. He doesn't tell them why. Then he goes to each man alone and says the same thing: write for me the Torah of Moses your teacher. In Greek. Seventy-two rooms. Seventy-two pens. No way to compare notes. If you've ever translated anything, even a text message for a grandparent, here is the problem. A sentence can have more than one right answer. So what comes out of those seventy-two rooms?
screen: `SEVENTY-TWO ELDERS.` → `SEVENTY-TWO SEPARATE HOUSES.` → `WRITE FOR ME THE TORAH.`

segments.voice: The same thing, every time. The Talmud says God put wisdom in each one's heart, and all of them agreed. Even more: each one made the same small changes, in places where a word-for-word Greek version might be misread by a king. The very first line is one of them. Hebrew opens with the word for in the beginning, then created, then God. Read too literally, a Greek reader might think in the beginning was the one doing the creating. So all seventy-two wrote it as God created in the beginning. In the legend, careful translation is a kind of guarding. And the rabbis had more than one feeling about it. In the Mishnah, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that besides Hebrew, the holy books may be written in Greek. The Talmud finds a reason in Genesis, in Noah's blessing. In the King James words: "God shall enlarge Japheth, and he shall dwell in the tents of Shem." The rabbis read it as the beauty of Japheth, the Greek language, dwelling in the tents of Shem, Israel's house of study. But the minor tractate Soferim remembers a Greek translation made for King Ptolemy as a hard day, as hard for Israel as the day the golden calf was made, because the Torah could not be fully translated. Both memories sit in the tradition side by side. A gift that lets the Torah travel. A loss, because something always stays behind in the original. Anyone reading a verse in English today is standing inside the old Jewish argument about what that costs and what it gives.
screen: `ALL SEVENTY-TWO AGREE.` · `GOD CREATED IN THE BEGINNING.` · then, large: `GOD SHALL ENLARGE JAPHETH.` · `A GIFT, AND A HARD DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: read a verse in a translation. If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, pick one short verse, any verse. Read it once slowly in your own language. Then sit with it, and ask: which word here might be carrying something it can't quite hold? Which word would you want to see in the original? If you know a little Hebrew, look at the Hebrew too, and notice the difference without judging either one. If you don't have a verse at hand, use Noah's blessing from today. If you pray, you can use words from your tradition to give thanks for whoever carried this text into your language. The bell holds the time.
Megillah, the Talmud tractate that tells how seventy-two elders in separate rooms all wrote the same Greek translation of the Torah. Today's word.

Your line: something always stays behind in the original. That ends a week that began with three parts, one library, then a doubt didn't throw a book out, plain meaning first, where the verse breathes is where its thought divides, the pages ran out, the handing-on didn't, and two cultures meet. Today, thank one translator in your mind. Day eight hundred eighty-nine.

options: translate it word for word and let the king read it as he likes.
write it as God created in the beginning.
fork.reveal: the Talmud says all seventy-two, in separate rooms, wrote God created in the beginning. the same careful change, everywhere.

original.note: Hebrew: the Greek language, the one tongue the Mishnah's Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel allows besides Hebrew for holy books.

trapdoor: what you thought: a translation is just the same book in another language.
what it means: the rabbis remembered the Greek Torah as both a gift and a loss: it traveled, and something stayed behind.

what a scholar hears: Megillah 9a tells of seventy-two elders in separate houses making the same changes; Megillah 9b grounds Greek in Noah's blessing of Japheth; Soferim compares the day to the golden calf.
